prompt: A friend says their synth sounds "more hi-fi" because they turned the output volume up. Which setting actually determines the highest frequency a digital signal can represent?

options.explanation: Correct. The sample rate sets how often the signal is measured, and the highest representable frequency is half of it.
Bit depth sets how finely each sample's value is recorded, which affects the noise floor, not the frequency limit.
Volume scales the sample values; it changes neither the frequency limit nor the resolution of the format.
Block size affects how often the audio callback runs and the processing deadline, not the frequency content.

workedExample:
Keep three settings apart:

| Setting | Controls |
|---|---|
| Sample rate | How often: frequency limit (half the rate) |
| Bit depth | How finely: noise floor |
| Level | How big relative to full scale |

The frequency limit is half the sample rate: 24 kHz at 48 kHz. The Nyquist-limit unit explains why.

prompt: You double an audio block’s sample count while keeping the sample rate unchanged. How does its processing deadline change?

options.text: The callback gets half as long
options.explanation: Twice as many samples take twice as long to play at the same rate.

options.text: It gets twice as long per block, but each block also contains twice the work
options.explanation: Correct. Larger blocks relax callback frequency, without automatically increasing processing capacity per sample.
The hardware still consumes samples at a fixed rate.

options.text: It equals the complete input-to-output latency
options.explanation: A block duration is a processing budget; converter and other buffering delays also affect latency.

workedExample: A block covers more audio time when it contains more samples at the same rate. All processing must still finish before the block is consumed, with safety margin. Larger blocks trade callback overhead and buffering delay rather than creating free computation.

prompt: A mono float32 delay buffer fits in RAM. You switch it to stereo with the same sample rate and maximum delay. What happens to buffer memory?

options.explanation: Stereo stores two channels rather than one.

options.text: It stays the same because the duration is unchanged
options.explanation: Memory depends on channel count as well as duration and sample format.
Correct. Each channel needs its own samples for the same duration.

options.text: It grows eightfold because bits become bytes
options.explanation: The bytes per float32 sample have not changed.

workedExample: The buffer stores samples for the entire delay in every channel. Stereo doubles channel count while rate, duration and bytes per sample remain fixed. Check total RAM, including other synth state, before adding the feature.
